module_title: Information Processing & Memory: The Brain as a Computer (Foundational)
introduction: This foundational level introduces the Information Processing Theory, a cognitive approach that compares the human mind to a computer. It covers the three fundamental steps of memory and the highly tested Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model of memory.

core_concepts.title: What is Information Processing Theory?
core_concepts.description: Information Processing Theory (prominently associated with George Miller) views learning as a cognitive process where the brain takes in information, processes it, stores it, and retrieves it when needed. Unlike Behaviorism (which focuses on outward actions), this theory focuses entirely on the internal mechanics of the mind.

core_concepts.title: The Three Steps of Memory
core_concepts.description:
For learning to be permanently stored, it must pass through three distinct stages:
1. Encoding: The process of receiving sensory input and transforming it into a format (code) that the brain can understand and store.
2. Storage: Holding onto the encoded information over time.
3. Retrieval: Accessing and bringing the stored information back into conscious awareness when needed.

core_concepts.title: Atkinson-Shiffrin Multi-Store Model
core_concepts.description:
The classic model divides memory into three distinct stores:
1. Sensory Memory: The earliest stage. Holds sensory information (Iconic = visual, Echoic = auditory) for a fraction of a second. If you don't pay attention to it, it is immediately lost.
2. Short-Term Memory (STM): Information you pay attention to moves here. It holds a limited amount of info (about 15-30 seconds) unless rehearsed.
3. Long-Term Memory (LTM): If STM is meaningfully rehearsed, it moves to LTM. LTM has unlimited capacity and can store information for a lifetime.

core_concepts.title: George Miller's Magic Number
core_concepts.description: In 1956, George Miller proved that the capacity of Short-Term Memory is limited to exactly '7 plus or minus 2' items (i.e., 5 to 9 items). This is why traditional phone numbers were designed to be 7 digits long. To hold more, the brain uses 'Chunking' (grouping individual pieces of info into larger, meaningful units).

important_entities.name: Chunking
important_entities.key_fact: A pedagogical strategy to bypass the limits of Short-Term Memory.
important_entities.significance: Instead of memorizing 10 individual numbers (9-8-7-6-5-4-3-2-1-0), which exceeds the 7+/-2 limit, a student chunks them into three groups (987-654-3210). This turns 10 items into 3 items, making it easily fit into STM.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners often test the difference between types of rehearsal. **Maintenance Rehearsal** is simply repeating a word over and over (rote memorization). It keeps info in STM but is poor for transferring to LTM. **Elaborative Rehearsal** involves linking new information to things you already know. Elaborative rehearsal is required to securely move information into Long-Term Memory.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember the sequence of a computer saving a file: First you type it (Encode), then you save it to the hard drive (Store), then you open it later (Retrieve).

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a question asks what limits a child's ability to hold multiple instructions in their head at once, the answer relates to the limited capacity of **Short-Term/Working Memory**.
